culture.fact: In Wisconsin a Bloody Mary traditionally arrives with a small free beer on the side to chase it. A Wisconsin historian told WUWM that beer chasers were established before Bloody Marys caught on in the 1950s, and that the custom exists in Minnesota, Iowa, Illinois and Michigan but its heart is Wisconsin.

That little beer is called a 'snit.' Brian Bartels, the Wisconsin-raised author of 'The Bloody Mary' (Ten Speed Press), describes it as about a 3 oz pour, an example of 'tandem drinking' like a boilermaker. InsideHook dates the snit ritual to sometime in the 1980s.

Chaser beers vary by bar: a baby Miller High Life (Honeypie), a short Rhinelander or Hopewell's 8 oz 'Lil' Buddy' can, Spotted Cow (Eldr+Rime), or Miller Lite in a little plastic cup (Sobelman's). Bay View bartender Matt Langoehr compared it to the water back served with bourbon.

Milwaukee's garnish arms race has a start date. In 2012 Dave Sobelman stuck a cheeseburger slider on a skewer in a Bloody Mary and posted it on Facebook; the post went viral and set off an unspoken competition among Milwaukee bars. His earlier garnishes came from the neighboring Bay View Packing plant.

Sobelman's 'Bloody Beast' began in 2014 as a joke when a server brought in an 80-ounce Mason jar. It's now a whole fried chicken on an 80 oz bloody ($65 in 2026). Up to a third of Sobelman's business is Bloody Marys, and about half its weekend crowd is from out of town.

Wisconsin didn't invent the Bloody Mary, and no research proves meat-tower garnishes started there, but Bartels credits the state as the likely source of the beer chaser. Historian Jim Draeger worried the chaser is fading as elaborate garnishes take center stage.

The Bloody Mary's origin is contested. Fernand 'Pete' Petiot is usually credited, from Harry's New York Bar in Paris around 1921 and later the St. Regis King Cole Bar in New York, where it was renamed the 'Red Snapper'. George Jessel claimed a 1927 Palm Beach invention, and the earliest print reference to a 'Bloody Mary' as half tomato juice, half vodka is a December 1939 Lucius Beebe column.

The Caesar is Canada's cousin of the bloody. Bartender Walter Chell created it in 1969 at the Calgary Inn for the opening of its Italian restaurant, Marco's, inspired by spaghetti alle vongole. He mashed clams into a 'clam nectar' for the tomato base, and Canadians now drink more than 400 million Caesars a year.

Clamato (tomato juice with clam broth) was introduced by the Duffy-Mott Company in 1969, the same year as the Caesar, and is now the standard Caesar base. Chell told the Toronto Star his secret was a dash of oregano, and that he didn't use Tabasco.

Milwaukee crowns bloodies every year. 'MKE's Best Bloody,' a benefit for the Great Lakes Hemophilia Foundation, held its 14th edition on March 1, 2026 at 3rd Street Market Hall: Best Overall went to Patti's Power Plant, Most Inventive to Red Maple MKE, Most Milwaukee to Burnsie's Bar & Grill, and Most Like a Meal to Smokin' Jack's BBQ. It raised more than $55,000. Separately, the Bloody Mary Festival-Wisconsin held its 6th edition at the Harley-Davidson Museum on June 21, 2025.

Wisconsin's other brunch-adjacent drink is the Brandy Old Fashioned, the unofficial state cocktail. It's made with muddled sugar, orange, cherry and bitters, a heavy pour of cheap domestic brandy (typically Korbel), and ordered 'sweet,' 'sour' or 'press.' It's a staple of the state's roughly 250 supper clubs.
Odd but true: Wisconsin makes a cheddar-cheese-flavored vodka called Cheddka, sold only in-state as of early 2026 and pitched for Bloody Marys.

One origin story credits Michel Ésper at the Club Deportivo Potosino in San Luis Potosí in the 1960s. He asked for beer with lime, salt and ice, and members started ordering 'Michel's limonada', which was shortened to 'michelada'.

culture.fact: The other popular etymology reads 'michelada' as a mash-up of 'mi chela helada', meaning 'my ice-cold beer'. 'Chela' is Mexican slang for beer.
culture.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelada (citing Los Angeles Times 2003 and Texas Monthly 2014)

culture.fact: A chelada is the simple version: beer, lime and salt. A michelada adds spice and a juice or purée such as Clamato, tomato or hot sauce, though usage varies by region. Budweiser's 2008 'Chelada' was the first prepackaged michelada-style drink sold in the US.
Clamato in its modern form was launched by Duffy-Mott in 1966 as a Manhattan clam chowder-inspired tomato cocktail. Keurig Dr Pepper now owns it, and in Mexico it is a standard michelada mixer.

Red beer (light lager plus tomato juice) is an upper-Midwest staple, especially in Nebraska and Minnesota. It also goes by Red Eye, Red Rooster, Red Draw, Bloody Beer and Montana Mary, and some drinkers add a raw egg.
Red beer is typically a morning or early-afternoon drink. One theory ties it to canned tomato juice, which became widely available in the 1930s and '40s.

Wisconsin's tomato-and-beer ritual is the 'chaser' or 'snit', a short glass of beer served alongside a Bloody Mary. Bartenders outside Wisconsin and parts of Minnesota often don't know the custom, and Milwaukee bars pour Miller Lite, Schlitz or a pony of Miller.

recipes.name: Bloody Mary (Difford's recipe)

ingredients.item: amontillado sherry (Difford's specifies Lustau Los Arcos)
Tabasco or other vinegar-based red hot sauce

steps: Chill a Collins glass.
Muddle the bell pepper in the base of a shaker.
Add the remaining ingredients and ice, then roll the drink between the shaker halves rather than shaking it.
Fine strain into the glass over fresh ice (straight from the freezer, to limit dilution).
recipes.rim: Optional: moisten the outside edge with lime juice and dip in salt (celery salt works well).

recipes.name: Bloody Maria

ingredients.item: Tabasco or other vinegar-based red hot sauce

steps: Chill a Collins glass, then rim it (see rim).
Roll all ingredients with ice between shaker halves; do not shake.
Strain into the glass over fresh ice.
recipes.rim: Moisten the outside edge with lime or orange juice and dip in salt mixed with cracked black pepper.

recipes.name: Classic Caesar
steps: Rim a tall glass with celery salt (or Clamato rimmer).
Add the vodka, hot sauce, Worcestershire and cracked pepper.
Fill the glass with ice and top with Clamato.
Stir well and garnish.
recipes.source_name: Mott's Clamato (Canada); the same build appears in The Canadian Encyclopedia's Caesar entry. Difford's Bloody Caesar is a stronger alternative: 2 oz vodka, 4 oz Clamato, 1/2 oz lemon juice, 7 drops Tabasco, 3 dashes Worcestershire, celery salt and pepper.

recipes.name: State Street Bloody Mary (Wisconsin-style, with a snit)

ingredients.item: vodka (Bartels prefers Wisconsin's Death's Door; any clear spirit works)
State Street Bloody Mary mix (batch below)
freshly ground black pepper, to taste
beer, poured on the side as the snit

steps: Make the mix: combine all MIX ingredients in a large pitcher, then refrigerate in a sealed container (keeps up to two weeks; makes about 50 oz, or 10 drinks).
Combine the vodka and 5 oz of mix in a shaker tin.
Roll between two tins several times to combine.
Pour into a rocks glass filled with ice and top with black pepper.
Garnish, and serve with a 3 oz beer snit on the side.
garnish_ideas: cured meats on a skewer (the published garnish)

Milwaukee load-out suggestions, not part of the published recipe: Wisconsin cheese curds, beef stick, pickle spear, pickled Brussels sprout, pickled asparagus, shrimp, bacon, olive, and a cheeseburger slider on top if you're going full Sobelman's
recipes.rim: None in the published recipe; celery salt is the classic Wisconsin choice.
recipes.snit_suggestion: A short pour of a light lager: Miller High Life, Spotted Cow or Lakefront Riverwest Stein, as Milwaukee bars do.
recipes.source_name: Brian Bartels (author of 'The Bloody Mary'; learned to bartend on State Street in Madison, WI), via PUNCH

recipes.name: Michelada (Dressed Up Mexican Beer)

ingredients.item: kosher or sea salt, for the rim
hot sauce such as Tabasco, Cholula or Valentina (optional, for michelada especial)
salty sauce such as soy sauce, Worcestershire or Maggi (optional)

steps: Spread salt on a small plate, rub the mug rim with the lime wedge, and dip the rim in the salt.
Basic version: add ice if using, pour in the lime juice, then the beer.
Michelada especial: add the optional seasonings to the salted mug, stir lightly, then pour in the beer.

recipes.name: Michelada con Camarones (Clamato michelada with shrimp)

ingredients.item: lime juice, plus extra for the rims
chile powder, for the rims and shrimp

steps: Pour lime juice onto one plate and chile powder onto another; dip the rims of four pint mugs in lime, then chile powder.
Dip the tops of the shrimp in chile powder and set aside.
Blend the Clamato, lime juice, orange juice, Worcestershire, pepper, salt, garlic and serrano until smooth.
Divide the mixture among the mugs, fill with ice, and top each with a lager.
Thread 6 shrimp onto each of 4 skewers and rest one across each mug.

recipes.name: Red Beer Deluxe (Midwest red beer)

ingredients.item: light lager (Busch Light, Coors Light or Grain Belt suggested; Miller Lite or Schlitz for a Milwaukee touch)

steps: Combine the beer, tomato juice and olive brine in a chilled mug.
Add the green olives and the salt.
Garnish with two dill pickle slices.
recipes.note: No published Wisconsin-specific red beer recipe was found. This upper-Midwest version from Punch is the closest reputable one. The light-lager-plus-tomato-juice base matches VinePair's and Chowhound's descriptions of the regional drink, and the Milwaukee beer substitution is my suggestion, not Punch's.
